newsitem.title: EGYPT: Egypt sentences four Moslem militants to gallows.
newsitem.headline: Egypt sentences four Moslem militants to gallows.

text.p: An Egyptian military court on Sunday sentenced four Islamists to the gallows for bombing a tourist bus and machinegunning a Cairo cinema.

Army judge Brigadier Faisal Heyba sentenced another 13 members of Egypt's largest and most active Moslem militant group, the Gama'a al-Islamiya (Islamic Group), to jail terms from five years to life in prison. Two militants were acquitted.
Frenzied defendants chanted Islamist slogans after the judge pronounced the four death sentences in the barn-like courtroom, in the desert 40 km (25 miles) northeast of Cairo.
Dressed in white, the colour signifying burial in Islam, they embraced, wept and shouted at the impassive soldiers lining the prosecution cage.
"Despite the courts and despite the injustice, Islam will return to Egypt," they boomed. "Sentences and the gallows will not keep us away from Islam."

The 19 defendants were charged with belonging to a Moslem militant group. Other charges included bombing a busload of Austrian tourists and attacking a Cairo cinema with machinegun fire in December 1993.
The public prosecutor had said in October the men killed police Colonel Ahmed Shalaan outside his home in Cairo in 1994 and the group had also attempted to assassinate other key political figures.
Egyptian President Hosni Mubarak has usually referred Moslem militants for trial in military courts because of their speedy proceedings.
But state security courts often hold trials for Islamists as well and death sentences are common. Egypt has so far sentenced more than 70 people to death in its struggle with the Islamists.

The Gama'a has been fighting the government since 1992 to transform Egypt into a strict Islamic state. The political violence, which peaked in 1993 and 1994, has claimed the lives of more than 1,000 people and wounded hundreds more.
The group targets tourists, high-ranking Egyptian officials and policemen in its attempts to destabilise the government.

Security crackdowns have largely confined their activities to the country's southern provinces although the group said it massacred 18 Greek tourists in Cairo last April in one of its bloodiest attacks in four years.

Barred from the courtroom on Sunday, relatives of the defendants anxiously waited outside for news. Several women pleaded with the guards to let in what they said were baskets of food for the defendants to break their Ramadan fast.

"They tortured me and electrocuted me to tell them where my son was and I didn't and I didn't even feel the pain. Now they've really killed me," wailed the mother of Yasser Turk who was sentenced to death.
"When will this injustice ever end? When will we be free to pray and be good Moslems?" wept another woman totally shrouded in black.
"Only when Mubarak dies," another relative calmly told her. "When he goes we will be free."
